drug_class: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptor blocker / biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (bDMARD)
purpose: Tocilizumab is used to treat certain types of arthritis, including rheumatoid arthritis, as well as some conditions that cause severe inflammation throughout the body. It is also used for giant cell arteritis, a condition that inflames blood vessels, and for serious immune reactions caused by certain cancer therapies. In some cases, it has been used to treat severe COVID-19 inflammation.
how_it_works: Your immune system makes a protein called interleukin-6 (IL-6), which can cause inflammation. In some conditions, your body makes too much of it, leading to painful swelling and damage. Tocilizumab blocks the place where IL-6 attaches in your body, like putting a cap on a lock, which helps reduce that harmful inflammation and relieves your symptoms.
common_side_effects: Upper respiratory infections like the common cold, headache, high blood pressure, elevated liver enzymes (usually found on blood tests), stomach pain, and reactions at the injection site such as redness or itching. Some people may also experience a rise in cholesterol levels.
warnings: This medication lowers your immune system, which means you are more likely to get serious infections — including tuberculosis (TB), fungal infections, and bacterial infections. Your doctor will test you for TB before starting. You should not take this medication if you have an active infection. It can also cause liver problems, tears in the stomach or intestines (especially if you take NSAIDs or steroids), and low blood cell counts. Tell your doctor right away if you develop fever, chills, unusual tiredness, or stomach pain. Live vaccines should be avoided while on this medication.
typical_dosing: For rheumatoid arthritis, it is given either as an intravenous (IV) infusion at a clinic every 4 weeks, or as a subcutaneous (under-the-skin) injection at home every 1 to 2 weeks depending on your dose. The exact dose depends on your weight, the condition being treated, and how well you respond. Your doctor will determine the right schedule for you.
